# Industrial Services Unit — Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment and Plan
## Diagnosis, Twelve-Month Plan, Exit Alternatives and Decision Architecture

**Version 2.0 — complete for decision. For the Board Strategy & Investment Committee. Circulated in advance to the ISU Managing Director and leadership team, Group CFO, Group General Counsel, Group HR Director and the four divisional MDs whose accounts are affected by §6. Not yet for customer, employee, works-council or market communication (§13).**

---

### How to read this pack

Three notes, then the substance.

**On what this is not.** It is not a third restructuring proposal. Two have been attempted; both delivered cost reduction and neither closed the loss [F]. That is evidence, not misfortune, and §3 sets out what it is evidence *of*. This is not a criticism of the colleagues who executed those programmes — they did what was asked, and did it. It is a criticism of the question they were given.

**On numbers.** No verified financial data has been made available to us. Every figure in this pack is therefore either a named variable awaiting input, or an illustrative value used only to show how the arithmetic behaves. Illustrative values are marked *[illus.]* and carry no evidential weight. §3.6 is the data request schedule: source system, owner, delivery date. The Committee should refuse to argue about any number in this pack that is not sourced there.

**On dates.** The Board has given twelve months [F]. Twelve months is the deadline for *evidence*; it cannot also be the deadline for *decision*. A business sold in month twelve of a fourth loss-making year is sold badly, and a sale process *begun* in month twelve is a wind-down with a press release. We recommend a dual track from day one with the substantive gate at **Month 5** (§12), the twelve-month date preserved as the outer boundary, and earlier trapdoors (§10.7) that fire without waiting for the gate.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Run a genuine dual track. Build one fact base that serves both outcomes. Decide at Month 5 against a stated economic inequality, with operational criteria subordinate to it. Fix price and perimeter before attempting growth, and never shrink the perimeter without first mapping which fixed costs actually leave with it. Bind the centre — allocation, intercompany pricing and internal recruitment — because on the facts available the centre is inside the causal chain, and a plan that does not say so will fail for reasons no one writes down.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Diagnosis, headline | Cost-out has been delivered twice and absorbed twice. The loss is sustained by a four-term bridge in which **volume loss, price erosion, mix deterioration and fixed-cost under-absorption** interact; under-absorption is the term both prior programmes ignored, and it is why cost reduction larger than revenue decline still failed to close the gap (§3.2) [A][H] |
| Structural vs execution | **We decline to publish a split before the Month-2 fact base.** A split asserted now would be decoration. §3.3 gives the five tests that produce it and the classification into *execution-recoverable*, *structural-perimeter* (recoverable only by exiting) and *structural-permanent* |
| Primary risk, ranked 1 | **Demand.** The order book is shrinking [F]. That is share loss, price-led loss, customer in-sourcing, or end-market decline — §3.5 decomposes it. Any plan that treats the demand side as stable is not a plan |
| Primary risk, ranked 2 | **Capability drain.** Best managers transferring out, largely to sister divisions [F]. This is the risk turnarounds routinely under-manage, and it is partly self-inflicted by the Group (§7) |
| Primary risk, ranked 3 | **Going-concern doom loop.** Customers do not sign multi-year maintenance and inspection contracts with a supplier believed to be for sale. A visible dual track can accelerate the very decline it exists to arrest (§8) |
| Where profit plausibly is | Recurring maintenance on the installed base, regulated inspection and certification, spares/consumables attach, scheduled turnaround work — **only where route density and repricing rights exist** (§5.3) [H] |
| Where it plausibly is not | Staffed labour supply, capital installation, sub-density geographies, and legacy contracts without indexation. Group-linked accounts must be tested, not assumed (§5.4, §6) [H] |
| The shrink trap | Perimeter reduction is invalid without a **step-fixed-cost map** showing which costs leave, at what volume threshold, and what the remaining core must then carry (§4). Two prior programmes appear to have cut cost without moving this map |
| Centre's own obligation | Allocation freeze at Month 0; **arm's-length intercompany pricing with any concession charged to the benefiting division, not to ISU**; internal-transfer approval at Group CEO level plus transfer fee; 10-working-day board response standard (§9) |
| Cross-subsidy consequence, stated plainly | Repricing intercompany work **moves margin between divisions; Group cash is unchanged.** It makes ISU's P&L honest, not better. The Committee must accept this in writing or the turnaround will be a paper one (§6.3) |
| Decision rule | **Economic master rule** (§12.1): retain only if risk-adjusted NPV of turnaround, net of total cost-to-try and stranded cost, exceeds certain-equivalent net proceeds available now, plus quantified option value of retained customer access. Five operational gate criteria (§12.2) are *necessary but not sufficient* |
| Gate rule, unambiguous | **All five criteria must be met.** One 30-day cure, available once, on one named criterion, and only if the cash and retention criteria are both already met. Four-of-five is a fail (§12.3) |
| Exit alternatives | **Six, named and ranked in §11**: whole trade sale; sequential carve-out/break-up; sponsor platform sale; MBO/MBI with vendor support; JV/partial sale preserving Group customer access; managed run-off with contract novation |
| Total cost-to-try | Defined as an equation in §12.4: twelve months of operating loss + programme spend + restructuring cash + value decay of a delayed sale + stranded cost crystallised late. This single comparison is the reason the pack exists |
| Resourcing sought | Parameterised in §14.2. The one non-negotiable line is a **retention pool that pays on either outcome** — it is worthless as a retention instrument if it pays only on turnaround success |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.5, sought on **24 April** |
| Ownership | ISU Managing Director accountable for the turnaround track. A **separate, ring-fenced exit-track lead reporting to the Group CFO**, appointed within 15 days. One person cannot credibly run both, and asking them to will produce a compromised version of each |

### 1.1 Confidence, and the honest posture

A business that has cut cost twice without moving its loss is telling you that its problem is priced into its revenue and its capacity, not into its cost line [J, supported by the structure at §3.2]. The trap it has walked into twice is ordinary: cost-out is measurable, board-legible and within management's unilateral control, so it is what gets proposed. Price realisation, bid discipline, contract structure and perimeter are none of those things, so they get deferred. The result is an organisation that becomes progressively better at delivering cheaply the work it should never have taken.

We should say plainly, since it will be thought in the room in any case: **on the facts available, exit is at least as likely to be right as turnaround.** This pack is not written to defend the unit. If the Month-2 fact base returns as we suspect it may on density and repricing rights, we will say so in Month 2 rather than Month 12, and the Committee should hold us to that.

We would also ask that exit be described, from the outset and consistently, as an honourable outcome rather than a defeat. If the organisation believes that only turnaround counts as success, the fact base will bend, the gate will be argued rather than measured, and the people who matter will leave before Month 5.

---

## 2. The prior question the Board has not yet answered

### 2.1 "A credible path to profitability" needs a number

The Board's instruction is clear in intent and undefined in measurement [F]. Left undefined, Month 12 becomes an argument about momentum and goodwill — an argument incumbent management wins by default and the shareholder loses. We ask the Committee to ratify a definition on 24 April.

| Test | Proposed threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Run-rate profit | **EBIT ≥ 0 at the Month-12 exit run-rate**, on the perimeter *locked at Month 5*, before restructuring charges, after full arm's-length Group allocation | "Run-rate" prevents a flattering final quarter; "locked perimeter" prevents winning by redefinition; "full allocation" prevents winning by accounting |
| Cash quality | **EBIT-to-operating-cash conversion ≥ 70%**, with unbilled WIP days and contract-retention balances no worse than the Month-0 baseline | Services businesses can manufacture EBIT through WIP and percentage-of-completion recognition. Cash is the honest test |
| Trajectory | Contracted bridge to **ROCE ≥ Group WACC + 200bps within 24 months** of Month 12 | Breakeven is not an investment case. Zero is not a destination |
| Self-funding | **No incremental Group cash from Month 9**, within the approved envelope | Earliest reliable indicator; hardest to dress |
| Quality of the bridge | **≥70% of the identified bridge in signed, contracted or executed actions** — not pipeline, not plan | This is what distinguishes a turnaround from a forecast |
| Demand | **Rolling twelve-month book-to-bill ≥ 1.0 on the retained perimeter, split recurring vs project**, with recurring renewal rate ≥ target and realised-price-vs-target improving | Point-in-time book-to-bill in long-cycle contracting is lumpy; one renewal flatters it |

**Perimeter lock.** The perimeter is fixed by board resolution at Month 5 in a signed schedule naming contracts, branches, service lines and legal entities. Any subsequent change requires Committee approval and restates the baseline publicly. Without this, "EBIT ≥ 0 on the retained perimeter" is meaningless.

**A profitable shrinking business** — positive EBIT with book-to-bill persistently below 1.0 — is an orderly liquidation. That may be the right answer, but it should be called by its name and valued as such (§11, Option F).

---

## 3. Diagnosis: is this structural or execution?

### 3.1 What the two prior programmes tell us

Two restructurings reduced cost and did not reduce loss [F]. There are only four explanations, and they are not mutually exclusive:

1. **Savings were real but absorbed** by contribution lost to volume and price.
2. **Savings were partly notional** — announced gross, eroded by leakage, inflation, re-hiring, contractor substitution and one-off delivery costs.
3. **Cost left, capacity did not.** Headcount and SG&A were cut; depots, fleet, licences, bonding, QHSE infrastructure and IT remained. Volume fell against an unchanged step-fixed base, so **unit cost rose while total cost fell**.
4. **Mix worsened.** The work retained during decline was disproportionately the low-margin, price-competed work, because that is the work that is easiest to keep.

Explanation 3 is the one that reconciles the apparent paradox of "cost reduction larger than revenue decline, loss unchanged." It is also the one that neither prior programme was designed to address, and it is the reason a third cost programme would fail identically [J].

### 3.2 The bridge, as algebra rather than as assertion

We express the three-year deterioration as an identity so that the Committee can see which term is doing the work once real data arrives:

**EBIT₃ = EBIT₀ + (S·r) − (ΔV · cm) − ΔP − ΔM − U − R + ΔI − i**

| Term | Meaning | Source (§3.6) |

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |
| Likely gap | Vagueness. Autonomy without written scope reads as management failure, not freedom |
| Add | Precision — documented decision rights, thresholds, escalation triggers. More documentation produces more autonomy here, counter-intuitively |
| Drop | Motivational framing and aspirational language; actively corrosive of credibility |
| Failure mode | Formal structural objection: "not properly specified, and it touches co-determination" — and they will be right on both counts |
| 60-day indicator | Existence of a signed, unit-level decision-rights schedule; count of decisions taken against it |
| Watch item | **Works councils** — Betriebsrat, ondernemingsraad, Nordic union structures. Changes to appraisal criteria, working methods and monitoring are frequently co-determination matters. Engage as co-designers, not as clearance (§10.2) |
| Quiet opportunity | This cluster will build the best delegation architecture in the network. We would suggest letting it lead the design and having other regions borrow from it, rather than the reverse — a small reversal of the usual flow that would itself say something useful about the initiative |

### Card C — Latin Europe (FR, IT, ES, PT, GR)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Moderate-to-high authority distance; direct on substance, relationship-mediated in form; individual attribution with strong reputational weight; moderate ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Relational legitimacy. It must come from a leader people are personally loyal to, or it is noise from the centre |
| Add | Public named conferral (§4.

The framing instincts are strong — dual track from day one, a Month-5 real decision gate, self-binding conduct at the centre, and the cross-subsidy hypothesis are all the right moves and better than most packs of this type. But the document **fails as a deliverable** on three counts: it is roughly 15% written, its headline diagnosis contains an arithmetic contradiction, and it presents invented financial data as findings. Three of the four things the brief explicitly asked for are referenced by section number and never produced.

---

## 1. Critical: the deliverable is not delivered

The brief asked for four things. The document delivers one-and-a-half.

| Requested | Status |
|---|---|
| Diagnose structural vs execution losses | Partially — a headline split (55–60/40–45) asserted with no derivation method |
| Identify profitable customer segments and service lines | **Not delivered.** §5 exists only as a one-line teaser in the summary table |
| Turnaround plan with milestones for the one-year deadline | **Not delivered.** Four scattered dates; no workstreams, owners, sequencing or 30/60/90 |
| Exit alternatives and choice criteria | **Not delivered.** "Six, ranked" — none named. Choice criteria present only as the Month-5 operational gate |

The text stops mid-sentence-of-a-document at §2.1 while forward-referencing §§3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15. A reader receives a table of contents with an eloquent preamble. Everything below is secondary to fixing this.

---

## 2. Analytical errors and internal contradictions

**2.1 The headline bridge does not compute.** "$46M of cost reduction … overwhelmed by ~$42M of volume and price erosion." $46M > $42M. On these numbers the unit should have *improved* by $4M, not stayed loss-making for three years. Either the numbers are wrong, or a third term is missing — almost certainly **fixed-cost under-absorption as volume fell**, plus mix deterioration and restructuring charges. That missing term is not a rounding issue; it is the actual diagnosis, and omitting it makes the marquee conclusion unsupported.

**2.2 "Revenue-side" is silently equated with "recoverable."** Revenue erosion is frequently the *most* structural cause of failure: commoditisation, customer in-sourcing, technology substitution, loss of route density. The document uses revenue-side to argue against a third cost programme (correct) and then implies recoverability (unsupported). The structural/execution split needs a stated method — e.g. contribution margin per contract repriced at observed market-clearing rates, competitor cost-curve position, win/loss price gap analysis — not a percentage range with a promise to test it later.

**2.3 Direct contradiction with the case facts.** "Principal risk: **not** customer flight." The unit's order book is shrinking. That *is* customer flight, or price-led share loss, or both. Manager attrition is a serious risk and deserves the emphasis given, but declaring the demand side a non-risk while the order book contracts is an error a board member will spot in the first five minutes.

**2.4 The Month-5 gate is logically incoherent.** §1 says the gate has "five published criteria, **all** of which must be met." The failure test triggers at "**fewer than four** of five." Some carry an "illustrative" tag; the diagnosis line does not. ---

## 3. Substantive omissions the brief required

**3.1 Cost-to-serve and the shrink-to-core trap.** The plan says "shrink the perimeter first." It does not address what happens to the overhead the exited perimeter was absorbing. In industrial services this is the classic death spiral: every cut raises the fixed-cost burden on what remains, the next tranche turns unprofitable, and the unit shrinks to nothing while never reaching breakeven. A perimeter decision is invalid without a **step-fixed-cost map** (depot/branch, fleet, licences, QHSE, bonding, IT) showing which costs actually leave with which service line and at what volume threshold. The single $55–70M "stranded cost" figure is not a substitute.

**3.2 The going-concern doom loop.** Customers do not sign multi-year maintenance and inspection contracts with a supplier rumoured to be for sale. That single comparison is the pack's reason for existing and it is nowhere.

Better: a Group CEO-level approval requirement plus an internal transfer fee charged to the receiving division, paired with a *positive* proposition — guaranteed landing roles on either outcome, deal bonus, and explicit career credit for turnaround service. 1. **Write the missing 85%** — service-line and segment P&L method, the twelve-month milestone plan with owners, the six exit options with proceeds logic, and the decision architecture.
2. **Repair the bridge** and introduce the under-absorption term; re-derive the structural/execution split from a stated method.
3. **Strip or explicitly flag every invented number**; replace with a parameterised model plus a data request schedule.
4. **Resolve the four-of-five / all-five contradiction.**
5. **Add the economic decision rule** (risk-adjusted NPV vs certain-equivalent proceeds) as the master criterion, with the operational gate subordinate to it.
6. **Add** step-fixed-cost mapping, sector liability schedule, natural-owner/buyer universe, going-concern protection for customers, and total cost-to-try.
7. **Reconcile** the "customer flight is not the principal risk" claim with the shrinking order book — or drop it.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**

The Board's instruction is clear in intent and undefined in measurement. If it remains undefined, Month 12 becomes an argument about goodwill and momentum, which is an argument the incumbent management team wins by default and the shareholder loses.

We would ask the Committee to ratify a definition on 24 April. Our proposal:

| Test | Proposed threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Run-rate profitability | **EBIT ≥ 0 at exit run-rate of Month 12**, on the retained perimeter, before restructuring charges and after full arm's-length Group allocation | "Run-rate" prevents a one-off Q4 flatter; "full allocation" prevents winning by accounting |
| Trajectory | Committed bridge to **ROCE ≥ Group WACC + 200bps within 24 months** of Month 12 | Breakeven is not an investment case. Zero is not a destination |
| Cash | **Self-funding from Month 9**; no incremental Group cash beyond the approved envelope | The most reliable early indicator, and the hardest to dress |
| Quality of the bridge | **≥70% of the identified bridge in signed, contracted or executed actions** — not in pipeline, not in plan | This is the criterion that distinguishes a turnaround from a forecast |

| Cross-subsidy consequence, stated plainly | Repricing intercompany work **moves margin between divisions; Group cash is unchanged.** It makes ISU's P&L honest, not better. The Committee must accept this in writing or the turnaround will be a paper one (§6.3) |
| Decision rule | **Economic master rule** (§12.1): retain only if risk-adjusted NPV of turnaround, net of total cost-to-try and stranded cost, exceeds certain-equivalent net proceeds available now, plus quantified option value of retained customer access. Five operational gate criteria (§12.2) are *necessary but not sufficient* |
| Gate rule, unambiguous | **All five criteria must be met.** One 30-day cure, available once, on one named criterion, and only if the cash and retention criteria are both already met. Four-of-five is a fail (§12.3) |
| Exit alternatives | **Six, named and ranked in §11**: whole trade sale; sequential carve-out/break-up; sponsor platform sale; MBO/MBI with vendor support; JV/partial sale preserving Group customer access; managed run-off with contract novation |
| Total cost-to-try | Defined as an equation in §12.4: twelve months of operating loss + programme spend + restructuring cash + value decay of a delayed sale + stranded cost crystallised late. This single comparison is the reason the pack exists |
| Resourcing sought | Parameterised in §14.2. The one non-negotiable line is a **retention pool that pays on either outcome** — it is worthless as a retention instrument if it pays only on turnaround success |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.5, sought on **24 April** |
| Ownership | ISU Managing Director accountable for the turnaround track. A **separate, ring-fenced exit-track lead reporting to the Group CFO**, appointed within 15 days. One person cannot credibly run both, and asking them to will produce a compromised version of each |

### 1.1 Confidence, and the honest posture

A business that has cut cost twice without moving its loss is telling you that its problem is priced into its revenue and its capacity, not into its cost line [J, supported by the structure at §3.2]. The trap it has walked into twice is ordinary: cost-out is measurable, board-legible and within management's unilateral control, so it is what gets proposed. Price realisation, bid discipline, contract structure and perimeter are none of those things, so they get deferred. The result is an organisation that becomes progressively better at delivering cheaply the work it should never have taken.

We should say plainly, since it will be thought in the room in any case: **on the facts available, exit is at least as likely to be right as turnaround.** This pack is not written to defend the unit. If the Month-2 fact base returns as we suspect it may on density and repricing rights, we will say so in Month 2 rather than Month 12, and the Committee should hold us to that.

We would also ask that exit be described, from the outset and consistently, as an honourable outcome rather than a defeat. If the organisation believes that only turnaround counts as success, the fact base will bend, the gate will be argued rather than measured, and the people who matter will leave before Month 5.

---

## 2. The prior question the Board has not yet answered

### 2.1 "A credible path to profitability" needs a number

The Board's instruction is clear in intent and undefined in measurement [F]. Left undefined, Month 12 becomes an argument about momentum and goodwill — an argument incumbent management wins by default and the shareholder loses. We ask the Committee to ratify a definition on 24 April.

| Test | Proposed threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Run-rate profit | **EBIT ≥ 0 at the Month-12 exit run-rate**, on the perimeter *locked at Month 5*, before restructuring charges, after full arm's-length Group allocation | "Run-rate" prevents a flattering final quarter; "locked perimeter" prevents winning by redefinition; "full allocation" prevents winning by accounting |
| Cash quality | **EBIT-to-operating-cash conversion ≥ 70%**, with unbilled WIP days and contract-retention balances no worse than the Month-0 baseline | Services businesses can manufacture EBIT through WIP and percentage-of-completion recognition. Cash is the honest test |
| Trajectory | Contracted bridge to **ROCE ≥ Group WACC + 200bps within 24 months** of Month 12 | Breakeven is not an investment case. Zero is not a destination |
| Self-funding | **No incremental Group cash from Month 9**, within the approved envelope | Earliest reliable indicator; hardest to dress |
| Quality of the bridge | **≥70% of the identified bridge in signed, contracted or executed actions** — not pipeline, not plan | This is what distinguishes a turnaround from a forecast |
| Demand | **Rolling twelve-month book-to-bill ≥ 1.0 on the retained perimeter, split recurring vs project**, with recurring renewal rate ≥ target and realised-price-vs-target improving | Point-in-time book-to-bill in long-cycle contracting is lumpy; one renewal flatters it |

**Perimeter lock.** The perimeter is fixed by board resolution at Month 5 in a signed schedule naming contracts, branches, service lines and legal entities. Any subsequent change requires Committee approval and restates the baseline publicly. Without this, "EBIT ≥ 0 on the retained perimeter" is meaningless.

**A profitable shrinking business** — positive EBIT with book-to-bill persistently below 1.0 — is an orderly liquidation. That may be the right answer, but it should be called by its name and valued as such (§11, Option F).

---

## 3. Diagnosis: is this structural or execution?

### 3.1 What the two prior programmes tell us

Two restructurings reduced cost and did not reduce loss [F]. There are only four explanations, and they are not mutually exclusive:

1. **Savings were real but absorbed** by contribution lost to volume and price.
2. **Savings were partly notional** — announced gross, eroded by leakage, inflation, re-hiring, contractor substitution and one-off delivery costs.
3. **Cost left, capacity did not.** Headcount and SG&A were cut; depots, fleet, licences, bonding, QHSE infrastructure and IT remained. Volume fell against an unchanged step-fixed base, so **unit cost rose while total cost fell**.
4. **Mix worsened.** The work retained during decline was disproportionately the low-margin, price-competed work, because that is the work that is easiest to keep.

Explanation 3 is the one that reconciles the apparent paradox of "cost reduction larger than revenue decline, loss unchanged." It is also the one that neither prior programme was designed to address, and it is the reason a third cost programme would fail identically [J].

### 3.2 The bridge, as algebra rather than as assertion

We express the three-year deterioration as an identity so that the Committee can see which term is doing the work once real data arrives:
